scenes.title: Porto-Novo
scenes.subtitle: The great market and the trading street

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: Its altitude is approximately 38 m (125 ft) and it covers an area of 52 km².

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: In 1730, the Portuguese Eucaristo de Campos named the city "Porto-Novo" due to its resemblance to the city of Porto.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: In 1861, the British, who were active in nearby Nigeria, bombarded the city, which caused the Kingdom of Porto-Novo to accept the French offer of protection in 1863.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: In 1883, Porto-Novo was incorporated into the French "colony of Dahomey and its dependencies" and in 1900, it became Dahomey's capital city.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: From 1908, the king held the title of Chef supérieur.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: After Benin's independence in 1960, Porto-Novo retained its status as the official capital, while Cotonou emerged as the economic and administrative hub.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: The palace and the surrounding district was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on October 31, 1996 in the Cultural category.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: In 2007, as part of the development of tourist attractions in the city, two new monumental buildings related to Voodoo were constructed, financed by the Benin Chamber of Commerce (CCB) and designed by an architectural firm.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: The commune covers an area of 52 square kilometres (20 sq mi) and as of 2013 had a population of 264,320 people.

scenes.title: The place
scenes.text: Capital of the kingdom of Hogbonou, then of colonial Dahomey. A city shaped by the Afro-Brazilian architecture of the Agudas, freed people who came back from Bahia in the 19th century.
